connections.why: Material choice depends on the physical and mechanical performance properties of each material
A material's properties determine which shaping, forming and joining processes can be used
CAM and CNC machinery automate the manual processes and techniques used to make products
Each process carries hazards that must be controlled through safe working practices
Processes scale up into the one-off, batch and high-volume methods of manufacturing industries
CAD/CAM underpins modern high-volume manufacturing and computer-aided quality testing
Material selection, recyclability and biodegradability drive a product's environmental impact
User-centred design factors are shaped by the technological and industrial developments of each era
Anthropometrics, ergonomics and user needs inform how the NEA prototype is designed
Mass production and the global marketplace raise the sustainability issues cleaner design must address
Production planning and costing rely on collecting and modelling marketing and feasibility data
Protecting intellectual property and meeting standards links to consumer and safety legislation
Risk assessment is required by health and safety law such as the Health and Safety at Work Act
Project management strategies depend on the planning, costing and forward planning of information handling
Iterative design strategies and project management are applied when developing the NEA prototype
Students must build sustainability and environmental impact into their NEA design decisions
The specification produced from investigation drives the design ideas that follow
The final design solution is realised through practical making of the prototype
The finished prototype is tested and evaluated against its specification
Knowledge of materials guides the selection and working of materials in the NEA build
Process and technique skills are applied directly when manufacturing the prototype
Quality control and assurance principles inform how the prototype's accuracy is judged
